channel.title: TABI — Discover Japan
channel.description: Your guide to the real Japan — travel, culture, and the things worth bringing home.

item.title: Vegetarian, Vegan, Halal and Allergies: Eating in Japan With Restrictions
item.description: The hard part is not finding restaurants. It is that dashi is in almost everything savoury, and 'no meat' does not communicate that to anyone.

item.title: Accessible Travel in Japan: What Works Well and What Still Doesn't
item.description: Japan's rail network is one of the most accessible in the world, and its older streets and buildings are among the least. Both things are true at once, and planning around the gap is the whole task.

item.title: Fukuoka: The Japanese City That Gets Everything Right
item.description: An international airport eleven minutes from the city centre, the best ramen in the country, and street food stalls along the river. Fukuoka is consistently rated the most liveable city in Japan and consistently skipped by visitors.

item.title: Sendai and Matsushima: The Easiest Way Into Tohoku
item.description: Ninety minutes north of Tokyo by Shinkansen and almost nobody goes. A green city built around a warlord's legacy, and a bay of pine-covered islands that has been considered one of Japan's three great views for four hundred years.

item.title: Nagasaki: The Port That Was Japan's Only Window on the World
item.description: For two centuries, when the country was closed, one artificial island in Nagasaki harbour was the entire point of contact with Europe. The city that grew from that is unlike anywhere else in Japan — and it carries the second atomic bombing.

item.title: Getting From the Airport Into the City: Narita, Haneda and Kansai
item.description: Three airports, three completely different problems. The wrong choice at Narita costs two hours and the price of a nice dinner, and the decision is easier to make before you land than after.

item.title: The JR Pass in 2026: When It Saves Money and When It Doesn't
item.description: Since the 2023 price rise the pass stopped being an automatic purchase, and it gets more expensive again in October 2026. The arithmetic is simple, and for most itineraries it now says no.

item.title: Send Your Suitcase Ahead: How Takkyubin Changes a Japan Trip
item.description: Japan has a next-day courier network that will move your suitcase between hotels for the price of a decent lunch. Almost no visitor uses it, and almost every visitor should.

item.title: What a Japan Trip Actually Costs, Line by Line
item.description: Japan has a reputation for being expensive that is thirty years out of date in some categories and entirely accurate in others. Here is where the money really goes.

item.title: Where to Sleep in Japan: Every Accommodation Type, Honestly Compared
item.description: Business hotel, capsule, ryokan, hostel, minshuku, apartment. They are not points on a price ladder — they are different products, and the cheap one is often the right one.

item.title: Aomori and Hirosaki: Late Blossom, Big Festivals, Deep Snow
item.description: At the top of Honshu, the cherry trees flower when Kyoto has finished, the summer festival is the loudest in Japan, and the winter snow is measured in metres. This is the region that rewards going at the wrong time of year.

item.title: Okayama and Kurashiki: A Great Garden and a Canal District
item.description: One of Japan's three great landscape gardens, and half an hour away a merchant quarter of white-walled warehouses along a willow-lined canal that survived the war entirely intact.

item.title: Skiing in Hokkaido: Why the Snow Is Actually Different
item.description: Siberian air crossing a warm sea produces snow so dry it does not pack. That single meteorological accident is why skiers fly past the Alps to get to an island north of Japan.

item.title: Izumo and Matsue: The Oldest Shrine and the Quietest Coast
item.description: On the far side of the mountains from everything else, a shrine that predates written Japanese history, a castle that was never rebuilt because it never burned, and a garden ranked first in the country for two decades.

item.title: Matsuyama and Dogo Onsen: Japan's Oldest Hot Spring
item.description: A bathhouse mentioned in eighth-century chronicles, a wooden building from 1894 that reopened in 2024 after five and a half years of restoration, and a castle on a hill above both.

item.title: The 88 Temples: Walking the Shikoku Pilgrimage
item.description: Twelve hundred kilometres, eighty-eight temples and roughly six weeks on foot around an entire island. Most people do a fraction of it, and the fraction still works.

item.title: Okinawa: A Different Country That Happens to Be in Japan
item.description: Subtropical, formerly an independent kingdom, and shaped by the worst battle of the Pacific war and eighty years of American bases since. Okinawa is the part of Japan that is least like the rest of it.

item.title: Ginzan Onsen: The Snow Town That Had to Start Turning People Away
item.description: A single street of wooden inns along a river, lit by gas lamps, buried in snow. It became too photogenic for its own good, and the town now controls who can walk down it in winter.

item.title: The Yaeyama Islands: Closer to Taiwan Than to Tokyo
item.description: Four hundred kilometres beyond Okinawa's main island lies a group where the jungle reaches the water, the villages have coral walls and sand streets, and the night sky is the darkest in Japan.

item.title: Hakodate: The Port Town at the Bottom of Hokkaido
item.description: A morning market selling squid you catch yourself, a hillside of nineteenth-century foreign consulates, and a night view that Japan has been ranking against Hong Kong and Naples for a century.
